title: Runtime API Stability — First Aid Draft
content:
Purpose:
This is a lightweight, operator-focused 'first aid' runbook for common API stability problems we see in the runtime layer: request timeouts, 429 (rate limit) spikes, degraded streaming (partial or stalled streams), and sudden elevation in 5xx/4xx error rates.

Scope and intended use:
- For on-call SREs and runtime engineers during the first 60 minutes of an event.
- Not a full postmortem; use for triage and short-term mitigations only.
- Keeps a focus on reopening safe customer-facing traffic as quickly as possible while preserving observability for root cause.

Quick indicators (when to use this doc):
- Global API P50/P95 latency increases > 2x baseline OR queue depth rising across nodes.
- Error rate alert: > 5% 5xx in 10m on production route.
- Sudden burst of 429s from the gateway or from our internal rate-limiter metrics.
- Streaming sessions marked as "stalled" or clients reporting truncated streams.

High-level triage flow (fast):
1) Confirm: Check alerts, Grafana runtime overview, and logs for a correlated signal.
2) Scope: Is this single-region, single-pool, or global? Use routing and pool metrics.
3) Mitigate: Apply targeted throttles/fallbacks, increase headroom (if safe), or switch to fallback model/variant.
4) Observe: Ensure mitigating action reduces customer impact before wide changes.
5) Escalate: If unclear within 20 minutes or mitigation fails, escalate to on-call infra eng and runtime lead.

Run-card: Timeouts (requests hang or exceed deadline)
- Detection:
  - Prometheus query: increase in http_request_duration_seconds_bucket (p95/p99) or many inflight requests per pod.
  - Upstream signs: model-serving kernel stalls, heavy GC, or queued inference requests in worker metrics.
- Immediate mitigations (0-10m):
  1) Verify if timeouts are model-specific: check per-model latency in "model-latency" dashboard.
  2) If one model variant is bad, route traffic to next-compatible variant (Console -> Routing -> Canary fallback).
  3) If node-level saturation: cordon slow pods and allow autoscaler to spin new ones (kubectl: kubectl drain/cordon; scale deployment/rscaleset).
  4) Temporarily reduce maximum sequence length (if available via request override) for heavy customers to decrease token compute.
- Probes to run:
  - kubectl get pods -n runtime -o wide (look for CrashLoopBackOff, high CPU or OOM).
  - curl -v to gateway health endpoints for affected regions.
  - Check worker process threads and heap (ssh into node if dedicated pool).
- Notes:
  - Avoid mass restarts if KV cache warmup will cause a bigger spike; prefer draining and gradual replacement.

Run-card: 429 storm (rate-limits)
- Detection:
  - Gateway logs show surge of 429 responses; per-customer quota breaches in rate-limiter metrics.
  - Spike in 429s correlated with a specific API key or route.
- Immediate mitigations (0-10m):
  1) Identify offending API key(s) via gateway logs (tagged request_id/customer_id).
  2) Apply per-key throttles or short-term quota bump for critical customers only (Console -> API Keys -> Temporary increase).
  3) Activate backlog processing mode for long synchronous requests: move to async if supported.
  4) If global rate-limiter misbehaving, flip to degraded mode (local per-host enforcement) — consult rate-limiter runbook.
- Probes:
  - Query rate-limiter metrics: RL_errors_total, RL_denied_requests.
  - Check Redis/etcd latency if rate-limiter uses shared store.
- Notes:
  - 429 surges often caused by retry storms from customers or bad exponential backoffs; coordinate with CS to notify top users.

Run-card: Degraded streaming (partial/stalled/null frames)
- Detection:
  - Streaming sessions marked with status "stalled" or streaming throughput drop while non-streaming requests normal.
  - Client complaints about truncated outputs or long gaps between chunks.
- Immediate mitigations (0-15m):
  1) Verify gateway -> runtime TCP/HTTP2 conn health. Check connection resets in gateway logs.
  2) If the issue affects a model capable of non-streaming fallback, flip clients to full-response mode for affected customers.
  3) If the streaming broker (streaming-proxy) is saturated, failover to secondary streaming brokers or scale replica set.
  4) Short-term increase of streaming keepalive timeouts may mask root cause but buy time.
- Probes:
  - tcpdump sample on affected gateway host (coordinate with infra).
  - Streaming broker metrics: in-flight streams, chunk-latency, event-loop lag.
- Notes:
  - Be mindful: switching to non-streaming for chat UX degrades perceived latency but avoids partial messages. Communicate with CS for impacted customers.

Run-card: Elevated error rate (5xx spike or multi-route 4xx/5xx rise)
- Detection:
  - Global rise in 5xx across multiple routes or multiple models.
  - Error logs show same exception signature OR downstream dependency errors (e.g., model-serving container failing to load weights).
- Immediate mitigations (0-20m):
  1) Isolate by route and customer: disable problematic routes or roll back recent routing changes.
  2) If new deploy suspected, roll back the deploy (use canary rollback buttons in Console).
  3) If dependency (S3/KMS/Model-store) is failing, apply cached model fallback or serve from replica region.
  4) If errors are due to bad user payloads, activate request validation/strict-sanitization for a subset.
- Probes:
  - Search logs for exception hashes.
  - Check model-store latencies and s3 error metrics.
- Notes:
  - Keep sample request IDs for later replay and debugging. Do NOT expose customer data in public channels. Use secure artifact storage.

Useful queries and commands (quick reference):
- kubectl -n runtime get pods -o wide
- kubectl logs -n runtime <pod> -c runtime-server --tail=200
- Prometheus (examples):
  - http_requests_total{job="gateway",status="429"} increase over 5m
  - histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route))
- Gateway quick-check: curl -I https://api.redwood.ai/health
- Model serving: curl -X POST https://model-host.internal/v1/ping -d '{}'

Dashboards to open (high priority):
- runtime-overview (global) -> check regions/pools
- model-latency per-variant dashboard
- gateway-rate-limiter heatmap
- streaming-broker dashboard (chunk latency / in-flight streams)
- per-customer quotas dashboard

Escalation and comms
- If unresolved after 20m: ping #sre-oncall and @runtime-lead in Slack.
- For customer-impacting > 60m incidents, page the on-call product manager and CS exec.
- Use incident channel naming: inc-runtime-<YYYYMMDD>-<short> and keep a running bulleted timeline.

Post-incident short checklist (first 24h):
- Collect 10 representative request IDs and upload to secure S3 for replay.
- Add timeline to incident channel and mark who made mitigation changes.
- Decide if customer communications are needed (CS drafts).
- If mitigation involved config toggles or hotfixes, file a ticket to revert to long-term fix.
- Flag significant findings to "runtime-retro" weekly meeting.

Open questions / TODO (work-in-progress):
- Automate model-variant failover for known failure signatures (ticket: INF-1023).
- Can we add a safe circuit-breaker that reduces token budget per-request automatically during wide tail latency events? (design doc draft linked).
- Improve streaming instrumentation (per-chunk tracing id) to correlate client-side timeouts with server-side chunk creation.

Notes to self / operator tips:
- Prefer gradual actions over global restarts; cache warmup is a frequent secondary incident cause.
- When in doubt, route to the next-compatible model variant rather than immediate full-degrade to non-streaming.
- Keep a short list of top 5 customers by qps in your head during an incident. They matter.

Revision history:
- 2026-02-10: initial skeleton and run-cards (Aisha).
- 2026-02-24: added streaming broker mitigations (Connor).
- 2026-03-05: added rate-limiter degraded-mode info and TODO items (Lina).

End of doc.
